articles.title: Indian court releases 'cockroach' movement leaders from detention
articles.description: Leaders of India’s youth-led “cockroach” movement on Sunday pledged to press on with protests against the country’s election commissioner, hours after they were released from detention, as authorities sought to thwart major demonstrations in New Delhi. The rallies in the capital come after weeks of opposition mobilisation following allegations of misconduct during a nationwide voter roll revision that critics say could benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling party. The Election Commission of India, which oversees the voting process in the world’s most populous nation, has denied wrongdoing. Abhijeet Dipke, founder of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), and two other leaders were released Sunday, one day after they were detained when they landed in New Delhi to take part in a protest at the Jantar Mantar site in the heart of the city. Thousands of protesters have been detained since Saturday, according to the group and media reports. “We will not back down,” Saurav Das, another top CJP leader, told reporters after his release. “We urge people to come out and carry out peaceful protests,” he added, vowing to continue until Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar resigns. Smaller rallies took place in Delhi on Sunday. Dozens of protesters were detained near Jantar Mantar, which remained blocked off, AFP journalists witnessed. Police have not commented on the detentions. Reporters Without Borders (RSF) said at least 16 journalists had also been detained, calling the police actions “unacceptable”. “Covering events of public interest is not a crime,” RSF said in a statement. “It is their job.” In July, protests organised by the CJP over exam irregularities forced the resignation of the education minister, marking a rare climbdown by Modi’s administration. ‘Important show up’ Ahead of Saturday’s rally, authorities mounted a sweeping security operation across the capital, shutting down metro stations and more than 200 trains while imposing a ban on public gatherings in several areas. Thousands of police and paramilitary personnel remained deployed on Sunday, but metro stations reopened and previously restricted mobile services were restored. “I was detained for 10 hours yesterday,” said Aarti, 37, who gave only one name. “I have come again today because it is important to show up.” The protest leaders were released on the condition that they would maintain “peace for one year”, Ratna Singh, the CJP’s head lawyer, said in a social media post. The Supreme Court, hearing petitions challenging Saturday’s detentions and other security measures, directed the authorities to ensure protesters gathering peacefully were not detained illegally. “Detention shall only be after following a legal procedure,” Justice Joymalya Bagchi said in oral remarks. The court also ordered authorities to ensure there was no disruption to internet connectivity as seen on Saturday. ‘An embarrassment to India’ The CJP has emerged as one of the most significant political challenges to Modi during his third term in power, winning millions of followers on social media since it was launched in May as a satirical party. Soon after his release, the CJP’s Dipke took aim at Modi, calling him “an embarrassment to India”. “Never has this country seen a bigger coward and bully,” he said in a social media post. The revision of voter rolls resulted in more than 133 million names being removed from electoral lists, according to media reports. Critics say the measure has disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims, potentially benefiting Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party. Election authorities say the move was aimed at eliminating duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries. The detention of protesters on Saturday triggered sharp criticism and accusations that Modi’s government was stifling dissent. The UN human rights office called for the immediate and unconditional release of all those “arbitrarily detained” in Delhi — a comment the Indian government called “misplaced”. Rahul Gandhi, leader of the opposition Congress party, said he was planning to march to the Supreme Court on Monday with “every single person who believes in democracy”. “There is nothing to fear,” he said on social media. “These cowards can do absolutely nothing to us. “

articles.title: At least 139 migrants dead, including some children, after boat from Djibouti to Yemen capsizes, UN agency says
articles.description: At least 139 migrants, including at least 15 children, have died and around 84 are missing after a boat carrying more than 300 people capsized while sailing from Djibouti to Yemen, the United Nations’ International Organisation for Migration (IOM) said on Sunday. The boat, carrying 305 people, capsized near Guhere, north of Obock a port town in Djibouti during the night of Oct 8-9, the IOM said, citing survivor accounts. Around 82 people survived the shipwreck, the statement said. A spokesperson for the Ethiopian government did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Photographs shared by the UN agency showed worn-out sandals and sneakers washed up on the shore. A pair of shoes believed to belong to a migrant lies on the shore after a boat carrying about 305 people capsized while sailing from Djibouti to Yemen, according to the United Nations’ International Organisation for Migration on October 11, near Guhere, north of the port town of Obock, Djibouti, in this photograph released on October 10, 2026. — AFP “Our teams are on the ground alongside local authorities to provide emergency assistance,” said IOM Chief of Mission in Djibouti Alexandre Coissac. “This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities,” Coissac said. Djiboutian authorities are continuing search and rescue operations, the IOM statement said, adding that local authorities are also providing medical care to survivors and arranging burials for the deceased. The Djibouti government could not be immediately reached for comment. The migrants were heading to Yemen, with the hope of eventually making it to wealthier Gulf nations, even as Yemeni nationals themselves flee their country, which is experiencing the most serious escalation in fighting between Saudi Arabia-backed government forces and the Houthis since a UN-brokered truce in 2022. “Despite the violence in Yemen, migrants are still making the perilous journeys hoping to make it to the Gulf countries,” the IOM statement said. Fighting in Ethiopia Fighting has also broken out in Ethiopia since last month in the biggest escalation of violence since the 2020-2022 Tigray war. An IOM official told Reuters that the UN agency had documented heavy migrant traffic along the so-called Eastern Route through Djibouti for several years. “People continue to use the route amid changing conditions in Ethiopia and Yemen, although the volume and direction of movement can shift over time,” the official said. Ethiopian migrants interviewed as part of the agency’s most recent situation report on Djibouti from Sept 20-30 said they had left their country due to difficult living conditions, including the impact of drought. “Some migrants also reported that they were fleeing conflict and forced recruitment by armed forces,” the report said. This handout picture released by the International Organisation for Migration (IOM) Djibouti on October 11, 2026 shows members of IOM Djibouti assisting survivors after a boat sank off the coast of Djibouti on the night of October 8-9. — AFP Multiple residents of Tigray, where fighting erupted on September 23, have told Reuters that they had seen Tigrayan rebels forcibly recruit young men into the defence forces. The rebels have denied conducting forced recruitment. The conflict has sparked fears of a return to all-out war with Ethiopia and Eritrea severing relations over alleged Eritrean support for the rebel alliance seeking to overthrow Ethiopia’s government. Eritrea has denied backing the alliance. Severe risks The so-called Eastern Route presents many dangers, including accidents at sea, trafficking and arbitrary arrests once on land. In 2025, more than 900 migrants died or went missing along the route, according to IOMs Missing Migrants Project, as the number of people undertaking the journey increased by 18pc. IOM has described the crisis sparked by the fighting in Yemen as alarming, with displacement figures surging to 200,000 from 76,000 in mid-September, according to data released by the agency last week. More than 3,700 people have fled Yemen by sea to Djibouti as of last week, it said.

articles.title: Indian court releases 'cockroach' movement leaders from detention
articles.description: Leaders of India’s youth-led “cockroach” movement on Sunday pledged to press on with protests against the country’s election commissioner, hours after they were released from detention, as authorities sought to thwart major demonstrations in New Delhi. The rallies in the capital come after weeks of opposition mobilisation following allegations of misconduct during a nationwide voter roll revision that critics say could benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling party. The Election Commission of India, which oversees the voting process in the world’s most populous nation, has denied wrongdoing. Abhijeet Dipke, founder of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), and two other leaders were released Sunday, one day after they were detained when they landed in New Delhi to take part in a protest at the Jantar Mantar site in the heart of the city. Thousands of protesters have been detained since Saturday, according to the group and media reports. “We will not back down,” Saurav Das, another top CJP leader, told reporters after his release. “We urge people to come out and carry out peaceful protests,” he added, vowing to continue until Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar resigns. Smaller rallies took place in Delhi on Sunday. Dozens of protesters were detained near Jantar Mantar, which remained blocked off, AFP journalists witnessed. Police have not commented on the detentions. Reporters Without Borders (RSF) said at least 16 journalists had also been detained, calling the police actions “unacceptable”. “Covering events of public interest is not a crime,” RSF said in a statement. “It is their job.” In July, protests organised by the CJP over exam irregularities forced the resignation of the education minister, marking a rare climbdown by Modi’s administration. ‘Important show up’ Ahead of Saturday’s rally, authorities mounted a sweeping security operation across the capital, shutting down metro stations and more than 200 trains while imposing a ban on public gatherings in several areas. Thousands of police and paramilitary personnel remained deployed on Sunday, but metro stations reopened and previously restricted mobile services were restored. “I was detained for 10 hours yesterday,” said Aarti, 37, who gave only one name. “I have come again today because it is important to show up.” The protest leaders were released on the condition that they would maintain “peace for one year”, Ratna Singh, the CJP’s head lawyer, said in a social media post. The Supreme Court, hearing petitions challenging Saturday’s detentions and other security measures, directed the authorities to ensure protesters gathering peacefully were not detained illegally. “Detention shall only be after following a legal procedure,” Justice Joymalya Bagchi said in oral remarks. The court also ordered authorities to ensure there was no disruption to internet connectivity as seen on Saturday. ‘An embarrassment to India’ The CJP has emerged as one of the most significant political challenges to Modi during his third term in power, winning millions of followers on social media since it was launched in May as a satirical party. Soon after his release, the CJP’s Dipke took aim at Modi, calling him “an embarrassment to India”. “Never has this country seen a bigger coward and bully,” he said in a social media post. The revision of voter rolls resulted in more than 133 million names being removed from electoral lists, according to media reports. Critics say the measure has disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims, potentially benefiting Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party. Election authorities say the move was aimed at eliminating duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries. The detention of protesters on Saturday triggered sharp criticism and accusations that Modi’s government was stifling dissent. The UN human rights office called for the immediate and unconditional release of all those “arbitrarily detained” in Delhi — a comment the Indian government called “misplaced”. Rahul Gandhi, leader of the opposition Congress party, said he was planning to march to the Supreme Court on Monday with “every single person who believes in democracy”. “There is nothing to fear,” he said on social media. “These cowards can do absolutely nothing to us. “

The rallies in the capital come after weeks of opposition mobilisation following allegations of misconduct during a nationwide voter roll revision that critics say could benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling party. The Election Commission of India, which oversees the voting process in the world’s most populous nation, has denied wrongdoing. Abhijeet Dipke, founder of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), and two other leaders were released Sunday, one day after they were detained when they landed in New Delhi to take part in a protest at the Jantar Mantar site in the heart of the city. Thousands of protesters have been detained since Saturday, according to the group and media reports. “We will not back down,” Saurav Das, another top CJP leader, told reporters after his release. “We urge people to come out and carry out peaceful protests,” he added, vowing to continue until Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar resigns. Smaller rallies took place in Delhi on Sunday. Dozens of protesters were detained near Jantar Mantar, which remained blocked off, AFP journalists witnessed. Police have not commented on the detentions. Reporters Without Borders (RSF) said at least 16 journalists had also been detained, calling the police actions “unacceptable”. “Covering events of public interest is not a crime,” RSF said in a statement. “It is their job.” In July, protests organised by the CJP over exam irregularities forced the resignation of the education minister, marking a rare climbdown by Modi’s administration. ‘Important show up’ Ahead of Saturday’s rally, authorities mounted a sweeping security operation across the capital, shutting down metro stations and more than 200 trains while imposing a ban on public gatherings in several areas. Thousands of police and paramilitary personnel remained deployed on Sunday, but metro stations reopened and previously restricted mobile services were restored. “I was detained for 10 hours yesterday,” said Aarti, 37, who gave only one name. “I have come again today because it is important to show up.” The protest leaders were released on the condition that they would maintain “peace for one year”, Ratna Singh, the CJP’s head lawyer, said in a social media post. The Supreme Court, hearing petitions challenging Saturday’s detentions and other security measures, directed the authorities to ensure protesters gathering peacefully were not detained illegally. “Detention shall only be after following a legal procedure,” Justice Joymalya Bagchi said in oral remarks. The court also ordered authorities to ensure there was no disruption to internet connectivity as seen on Saturday. ‘An embarrassment to India’ The CJP has emerged as one of the most significant political challenges to Modi during his third term in power, winning millions of followers on social media since it was launched in May as a satirical party. Soon after his release, the CJP’s Dipke took aim at Modi, calling him “an embarrassment to India”. “Never has this country seen a bigger coward and bully,” he said in a social media post. The revision of voter rolls resulted in more than 133 million names being removed from electoral lists, according to media reports. Critics say the measure has disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims, potentially benefiting Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party. Election authorities say the move was aimed at eliminating duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries. The detention of protesters on Saturday triggered sharp criticism and accusations that Modi’s government was stifling dissent. The UN human rights office called for the immediate and unconditional release of all those “arbitrarily detained” in Delhi — a comment the Indian government called “misplaced”. Rahul Gandhi, leader of the opposition Congress party, said he was planning to march to the Supreme Court on Monday with “every single person who believes in democracy”. “There is nothing to fear,” he said on social media. “These cowards can do absolutely nothing to us. “

The boat, carrying 305 people, capsized near Guhere, north of Obock a port town in Djibouti during the night of Oct 8-9, the IOM said, citing survivor accounts. Around 82 people survived the shipwreck, the statement said. A spokesperson for the Ethiopian government did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Photographs shared by the UN agency showed worn-out sandals and sneakers washed up on the shore. Djiboutian authorities are continuing search and rescue operations, the IOM statement said, adding that local authorities are also providing medical care to survivors and arranging burials for the deceased. The Djibouti government could not be immediately reached for comment. The migrants were heading to Yemen, with the hope of eventually making it to wealthier Gulf nations, even as Yemeni nationals themselves flee their country, which is experiencing the most serious escalation in fighting between Saudi Arabia-backed government forces and the Houthis since a UN-brokered truce in 2022. “Despite the violence in Yemen, migrants are still making the perilous journeys hoping to make it to the Gulf countries,” the IOM statement said. An IOM official told Reuters that the UN agency had documented heavy migrant traffic along the so-called Eastern Route through Djibouti for several years. “People continue to use the route amid changing conditions in Ethiopia and Yemen, although the volume and direction of movement can shift over time,” the official said. articles.title: Governor’s rule and emergency imposed in KP — here’s what it means
articles.description: The federal government imposed an emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa amid growing tensions with the PTI-led provincial government, including disagreements over counterterrorism policy amid a deteriorating security situation in the province. The decision was taken under Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution of Pakistan. Here is what it means. Governor’s rule Article 234 of the Constitution of Pakistan stipulates that, if the president believes that a provincial government cannot function in accordance with the Constitution, the federal government can assume control of the province. This can be done either directly or by assigning the relevant functions to the provincial governor — hence the term governor’s rule. Under this arrangement, the powers of the provincial assembly can be exercised by Parliament. However, neither the president nor the governor can assume the powers of the high court or suspend its operations. Moreover, governor’s rule can be imposed for an initial period of two months, with a joint sitting of Parliament able to approve an extension of up to two months at a time. In total, governor’s rule can remain in place for a maximum of six months. While a province is under governor’s rule, its government or the chief minister cannot exercise their powers, but “I don’t see how it brings the government to an end”, said lawyer Mirza Moiz Baig. He added, “The government would come back into existence upon the end of the emergency”. “Once the proclamation expires, the Chief Minister and his Cabinet are restored,” lawyer Rida Hosain told Dawn . State of emergency Meanwhile, under Article 232, which pertains to the proclamation of an emergency, the provincial assembly continues to function as usual. However, if a provincial law conflicts with a federal law enacted by Parliament, the latter takes precedence. Lawyer Basil Nabi Malik, speaking to Dawn , explained that the chief minister would remain in office during a state of emergency. However, the federal government could assume certain functions of the provincial government. An emergency also allows the federal government to make provisions it considers necessary and suspend certain constitutional provisions relating to provincial bodies. However, as with governor’s rule, the federal government cannot assume the powers of a high court. It also empowers Parliament to confer powers and impose duties on federal government officers in the province. It further stipulates that laws passed by Parliament solely on account of the emergency will cease to have effect six months after the emergency ends. The proclamation of emergency lapses after two months unless it is approved by a resolution of a joint sitting of Parliament.

articles.title: Emergency, governor's rule imposed in KP as president approves cabinet decision
articles.description: Key developments: Emergency imposed under Article 232 , governor’s rule under Article 234 Cabinet recommended move due to KP govt’s ‘ deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism’ Technocratic council formed ; Fakhr Alam appointed as KP chief secretary PTI’s Gohar condemns decision as undemocratic, says peace cannot be established by weakening provincial autonomy Governor Kundi calls for unity for ‘new chapter’ in KP’s development ISLAMABAD: The federal government on Sunday imposed an emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa following the president’s approval of the recommendations by the federal cabinet. The measures have been approved under Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution, the President House said in a statement. The two provisions pertain to the proclamation of emergency and governor’s rule. Following the imposition, internet disruptions were being reported from parts of Peshawar, with Dawn unable to contact its correspondents there. According to sources in the telecom sector, mobile network and data services have been slowed or shut down in selected areas of some cities. However, there is no province-wide shutdown of mobile data or internet. Internet watchdog NetBlocks said network data showed a major disruption to internet connectivity in parts of KP as emergency was imposed. The federal government also authorised the deployment of Pakistan Army troops and assets in aid of civil power in KP. On the ground, shipping containers were placed around the city of Peshawar to block several roads, with heavy police deployment. The decision to impose the emergency provisions came during an emergency meeting of the federal cabinet chaired by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, where he was briefed on the security situation in KP. A statement issued by the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) said cabinet members reviewed the situation and took note of the “provincial government’s deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism”. The members proposed, given the “gravity” of the situation, that the PM advise the president to exercise “his constitutional authority and impose an emergency in the province under Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution”. The emergency imposition comes a day after PM Shehbaz met President Zardari and discussed the country’s overall security situation. That meeting came amid heightened tensions between the PML-N-led federal government and the KP government led by the PTI — which is in opposition in the Centre. They have been at odds over various issues, particularly on the counterterrorism policy, which was one of the main reasons behind the breakdown of their Oct 3 talks . The PTI has said it was being left out of security decisions concerning KP, which the Centre has denied . It also calls for reviewing the counterterrorism policy and opposes military operations. On the other hand, the Centre has been criticising the KP government’s efforts to combat terrorism in the province and objects to its stance on dialogue with the Afghan Taliban. It may be recalled that in July 2024, when Afridi’s predecessor Ali Amin Gandapur was the chief minister, the KP Assembly passed a resolution urging the federal government to consult with it and the provincial government before launching a new military operation. The resolution, passed by a majority vote, cautioned that proceeding without provincial consent could hinder the offensive’s success and result in adverse consequences, for which the federal government would be responsible. In December that year, the assembly voted unanimously against a potential military operation in parts of Khyber and Bannu districts. About a year later, after Afridi became the KP CM, the provincial assembly convened a grand jirga with Governor Faisal Karim Kundi and other parties in attendance. The moot unanimously demanded that the Centre prioritise negotiations with Afghanistan and consult the KP government over Afghan policy. Constitutional provisions Emergency Article 232 of the Constitution provides for the proclamation of emergency in a province. It says, “If the president is satisfied that a grave emergency exists in which the security of Pakistan, or any part thereof, is threatened by war or external aggression, or by internal disturbance beyond the power of a provincial government to control, he may issue a Proclamation of Emergency.” However, invoking this article “due to internal disturbances beyond the powers of a provincial government to control” requires a resolution from the provincial assembly of that province. In case the president “acts on his own” — which is not currently the case — the Proclamation of Emergency is to be placed before both houses of Parliament for approval by each house within 10 days. According to this provision, parliament “shall have power to make laws for a province, or any part thereof, with respect to any matter not enumerated in the Federal Legislative List” during the time of the proclamation of an emergency. Nothing in this Article shall restrict the power of a provincial assembly to make any law which the Constitution empowers it to make, but if any provision of a provincial law is repugnant to any provision of an Act by Parliament, the latter would prevail and the provincial law would be void as long as the parliamentary Act is in effect. Governor’s rule On the other hand, Article 234 deals with the imposition of the governor’s rule “in case of failure of constitutional machinery in a province”. For imposition of the governor’s rule, the president simply requires a request from the provincial governor, it says. “A proclamation issued under this Article shall be laid before a joint sitting and shall cease to be in force at the expiration of two months, unless before the expiration of that period it has been approved by resolution of the joint sitting and may by like resolution be extended for a further period not exceeding two months at a time,” the Constitution reads. However, it adds that no such proclamation shall in any case remain in force for more than six months. Article 233, which provides powers to the president to suspend certain fundamental rights during the emergency period, was not mentioned in the summary signed by President Zardari. Where is Sohail Afridi? A couple of hours after the imposition of emergency was announced, KP Information Minister Shafi Jan, who had been accompanying now dysfunctional KP Chief Minister Sohail Afridi on the PTI’s long march , claimed that the he had been taken into custody. Dawn contacted police for a confirmation soon after Jan’s claim, but there was no response. Meanwhile, MNA Shahid Khattak also claimed Afridi’s “arrest”, as well as MNA Junaid Akbar and others from there party. He also said he would be leading the march now. Later, the PTI issued a statement, condemning the “arrest” of Afridi and other and describing it as an act of “political victimisation and an attempt to weaken the province’s elected leadership and democratic institutions”. It quoted PTI spokesperson Sheikh Waqas Akram as saying that Afridi’s “arrest” could not be viewed in isolation from the federal government’s decision to impose emergency and governor’s rule. “The developments reflect a broader effort to bypass elected institutions and undermine the constitutional authority of the province. “The arrest of Chief Minister Sohail Afridi and Junaid Akbar has exposed the political nature of the federal government’s actions. These measures are not directed at addressing security challenges; they are intended to weaken PTI, undermine the elected government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and disregard the democratic will of its people,” he said. Akram demanded the “immediate and unconditional release” Afridi, Akbar and “all other political detainees arrested in connection with the ongoing action against PTI”. He also demanded that the federal government publicly disclose the “legal grounds, specific charges and procedural basis for the arrests of the chief minister and the PTI provincial president”. However, he sounded less certain while speaking on Geo News programme ‘ Naya Pakistan ’. He said they had received reports of Afridi and Akbar’s arrest, and adding that they were unable to confirm whether Jan and Khattak, too, had been taken into custody. “We are unable to contact some people […] Because the internet has been suspended in several areas, we are unable to contact. You do not know the havoc they have created in KP. People are escaping and going into hiding,” he said. In a clip shared on PTI’s official X account, Salman Akram Raja, the party’s secretary general, said, “We do not know where Sohail Afridi is, in what condition he has been kept. Junaid Akbar is also missing.” When Minister of State for Interior Tallal Chaudhry was asked about reports of Afridi’s arrest during ‘ Naya Pakistan ’, he said some individuals had been detained in view of the law and order situation but did not confirm whether they included Afridi. He said those who did not have a criminal record or were not wanted would be released. Council, chief secretary appointed Following the imposition of emergency, the federal government formed an 11-member technocratic KP Advisory Council to assist the governor with running the province. Later, Governor Kundi also chaired the first meeting of the council, vowing to restore peace in the province. Earlier in the day, the federal government appointed Dr Muhammad Fakhr Alam Irfan as the chief secretary of KP, according to an official notification, a copy of which is available with Dawn. The appointment will take effect immediately and remain in place until further orders, it said. Dr Irfan, a Grade 22 officer of the Pakistan Administrative Service (PAS), was previously serving as secretary of the Power Division in the federal Ministry of Energy. He hails from Mardan. In a separate notification, the federal government also placed Muhammad Yahya Akhunzada at the disposal of the KP government with “immediate effect and until further orders”. Akhunzada, a Grade 20 PAS officer, was serving as an additional secretary at PMO. He hails from Charsadda and has also served as additional political agent for North and South Waziristan, secretary of health, information and education in KP, and commissioner of Dera Ismail Khan. ‘Peace cannot be established by weakening provincial autonomy’ PTI Chairman Gohar Ali Khan strongly condemned the imposition of emergency in KP and “completely rejected” it. “This is an extremely alarming and grave political mistake and an undemocratic measure — the people will never accept such actions against their rights,” Gohar wrote in a post on X. He stated: “There is still time; this decision can be withdrawn in a few days. Let the federation set aside its ego, understand the ground realities, accept legitimate demands, respect the sentiments and emotions of the people, and save the country from further political and economic damage and from pushing back the democratic process. “Revisiting political decisions is not a sign of weakness but of wisdom in the national interest — otherwise, great damage will be done.” Stressing that the mandate of the people of KP was their constitutional and legal right, the PTI chairman said: “Peace cannot be established, nor stability brought, by ignoring this mandate, weakening provincial autonomy, and creating conflict between the federation and the province.” He asserted that there was “no disagreement on eliminating terrorism, but the fight against terrorism cannot be used as a justification to suppress the people’s voice, achieve political objectives, or limit the province’s constitutional authority”. “Terrorism can only be combated through national unity and a joint strategy,” Gohar maintained. “The federation cannot be strengthened by weakening the provinces. The solution to problems lies not in force, confrontation, and extraordinary measures, but in political wisdom, supremacy of the Constitution, and meaningful negotiations and practical steps.” The PTI chairman said his party will raise the matter on “every constitutional, legal, and democratic forum for the protection of the people’s mandate, provincial autonomy, and constitutional and democratic rights”. Later in the day, Gohar said PTI would challenge governor’s rule through the courts, assemblies and public forums. The PTI parliamentary committee held a meeting and categorically rejected the imposition of an emergency and governor’s rule in KP. In a statement issued afterwards, it termed the development “a direct assault on the public mandate and an unacceptable move”. “In a three-hour-long meeting of the PTI parliamentary party, the imposition of an emergency and governor’s rule in KP was strongly condemned and unanimously rejected. The meeting declared this step contrary to facts, unconstitutional, undemocratic, and a blatant insult to the public mandate of the province,” the statement said. “The parliamentary party made it clear that measures to render the elected provincial government ineffective and usurp its constitutional powers could pose grave threats to the federal system and democratic traditions. Such decisions will increase political instability and public unrest in the province, while already existing tensions between the federation and the province will further intensify,” it added. The statement added that the solution to political differences should be found through constitutional and democratic procedures and mutual consultation, rather than through force and coercion. It also raised serious questions regarding the conduct of the federal government. “The parliamentary party took the stance that if terrorism and the deteriorating law and order situation are the primary justification for the imposition of emergency, then why is the situation in Balochistan being ignored?” the statement asked. The meeting also made it clear that Afridi was the elected chief minister and a member of the provincial assembly. “Measures regarding his arrest, detention, or the usurping of his constitutional and democratic powers were strongly condemned. The meeting termed such actions an insult to the public mandate and a dangerous precedent for democratic traditions,” it said. The Tehreek-i-Tahafuz-i-Ayin-i-Pakistan (TTAP), of which PTI is a part, termed the move a violation of the Constitution. In a statement, the opposition alliance particularly assailed President Zardari’s PPP, claiming that the “most undemocratic actions and the imposition of governor’s rule” had been the hallmark of the party in the country’s history. “On the one hand, despite the extremely dire administrative and law and order situation in Balochistan, no such step has been taken, while on the other hand, this province — whose assembly and government stand on the true and real mandate of the people — has been targeted,” it contended. TTAP said it would convene a meeting on the matter and announce a joint course of action. Governor Kundi urges unity for ‘new chapter’ Meanwhile, Governor Kundi said the decision was made for “establishing peace in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, the prosperity of its people, and the development of the province”. “I am your governor, but beyond that, I want to play my role as a servant of this soil and a protector of your rights. Let us come together to bring peace to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and begin a new chapter of our province’s development,” he said in a statement. Kundi assured the public that it was his responsibility to raise their issues on the relevant forums. Recalling the sacrifices made in the fight against terrorism, he said, “Now the time has come that we do not let these sacrifices go to waste and together establish lasting peace in our province.” The PPP leader urged the public to set aside their political differences and unite for the province’s peace, the protection of its people, and the future of the coming generations. “We must not let our differences become an obstacle in the path of our province’s common interests.” Cannot allow PTI to destabilise the economy: PM tells cabinet Addressing the cabinet meeting, the premier said the PTI-led KP government cannot be allowed to derail the stabilising economy amid tensions between the two sides. “I will not allow them (PTI) to destabilise the economy,” he said during the meeting. On terrorism in KP and Balochistan, the premier said, “The way common citizens are being martyred, the way police officials and security officials, children and mothers [..] there can be nothing more heart-wrenching.” He recalled that Pakistan has repeatedly urged neighbouring Afghanistan to rein in the terrorist elements; however, “they still do not understand it”. PM Shehbaz also reiterated his condemnation of the recent deadly Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia, noting the long-standing fraternal ties between Saudi Arabia and Pakistan. “Our only goal is that peace should be restored in the region,” he said. “Pakistan expresses solidarity with Saudi Arabia and stands with it. We will not tolerate any aggression against Saudi Arabia,” he said, adding that it was a “red line” for Pakistan. During his address, PM Shehbaz also spoke of the recent staff-level agreement reached with the International Monetary Fund (IMF). “It is hoped that we will unlock the $1.2 billion tranche within this year,” he said, recalling a meeting with the IMF’s Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva at the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) last month. He commended the political and military leadership for “working together day and night” in bringing fiscal discipline to Pakistan. The premier recalled his visit to London last month, where he had met with senior executives from leading global financial institutions. He also spoke of Pakistan’s diplomatic efforts in the international community, taking note of the appreciation Pakistan has received for mediation in the Middle East conflict. “Pakistan continues to play its role with hard work and sincerity,” he said, particularly lauding the role of the Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir. Additional input by Ikram Junaidi, Kalbe Ali

articles.title: KP Governor's Rule: An emergency in the street and state
articles.description: Back in 2024, the political future of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and perhaps of Pakistan itself, looked like a coin toss. There were two broad possibilities. One was a grand political settlement, perhaps involving a period of exile for Imran Khan, with the United Kingdom replacing Saudi Arabia as the preferred destination. The other was the eventual termination of the last PTI provincial government through constitutional intervention. One of these possibilities has now materialised. There was a third option but this was not the 1990s when you could break a party with defections as its leader served time. No, political loyalties have not surged since, we just have tighter rules for turncoats. This gambit would not have worked in KP anyway. Floor crossing can’t be engineered when there has been a landslide. What we did not know back then was how the PTI government in KP could be dislodged when push came to shove. Indeed, only one of these options has come to pass two years later. The federal government has declared an emergency and Governor’s Rule. There are reports that Chief Minister Sohail Afridi has been arrested. The justification is a law-and-order situation, terrorism and the breakdown in negotiations with the government. The constitutional justification for federal intervention must be distinguished from its political rationale. Articles 232 and 234 provide extraordinary powers in different circumstances, and their invocation is subject to procedural requirements and limitations. A deterioration in security is an important consideration, but it does not automatically establish that constitutional government has become impossible. There is also the question of consistency. Balochistan, immediately south and southwest of KP, has experienced its own severe deterioration in security since the 2024 elections . The two provinces face different insurgencies and different political circumstances, but the comparison is unavoidable. If terrorism alone establishes the necessity for extraordinary intervention, why is the constitutional response different in Balochistan? This does not mean the security challenges in KP are imaginary, or that the provincial government bears no responsibility for its response. It means that the justification for governor’s rule must explain something more specific than the existence of terrorism. It must establish why the existing constitutional machinery could no longer deal with it. There is, however, another security crisis that helps explain the political context of this decision. It began in 2023, and its protagonists were not militants. May 9, 2023 May 9 remains consequential for Pakistan’s establishment in ways that subsequent and more lethal security incidents have not been. The attacks on military installations following Imran Khan’s arrest challenged assumptions about the relationship between the military and sections of the public that had traditionally been regarded as politically sympathetic to it. Since the Arab Spring began in 2010, Pakistan’s security establishment had reason to contemplate the possibility that mass mobilisation might produce consequences beyond the capacity of conventional political management. Pakistan had different institutions, a different political history and a military with a different relationship to the state, especially compared to say Egypt. The spectacle of governments losing control of public spaces, and sometimes their own institutions, had become part of the political imagination of the region. May 9 tested a version of that fear. The subsequent response suggested that the state possessed a greater capacity to suppress political mobilisation than PTI had anticipated. Arrests, prosecutions, restrictions on political activity and the disruption of party organisation altered the costs of confrontation. A serious underestimation had come to pass. The implications were particularly significant in Punjab. Although the May 9 incidents were concentrated in several parts of Punjab and KP, the attacks in Lahore carried considerable symbolic weight. A city long associated with the military’s institutional presence and political influence had witnessed an extraordinary breach. The state’s subsequent response changed the political environment in Punjab. Whatever the underlying level of support for PTI, public participation in confrontational politics became a much more consequential personal decision. The rules of political mobilisation had changed. Against this background, PTI’s victory in KP in February 2024 was an enormous morale booster. Despite the imprisonment of Imran Khan, the loss of its electoral symbol and substantial impediments to electioneering, the party demonstrated that its electoral appeal remained formidable. KP supplied PTI with something it had lost elsewhere: an elected government, an institutional base and a territory from which to organise its politics, but it also inherited the unresolved strategic problem of May 9. The failures of 2024 If there was uncertainty about PTI’s intended response, its choice of chief minister provided an early indication. Ali Amin Gandapur was a combative political figure, selected at a time when the party wanted to confront the federal government and demonstrate that its capacity for street mobilisation had survived. The threat of protest was that it would halt the business of the state. He attempted to deliver on that expectation. In October and November 2024, PTI organised major efforts to reach Islamabad’s D-Chowk, the second involving Bushra Bibi . Both ended in retreats, and the November confrontation involved casualties, injuries and a disputed account of the security operation: however, the consequences went beyond the failure to occupy a public square. For the federal government, the confrontations demonstrated that the capital could be defended against a determined political mobilisation. For PTI, they exposed the distance between the ability to assemble supporters and the ability to sustain a confrontation against a state willing to escalate. Gandapur too suffered the burden of May 9. The people in Punjab were no longer willing to protest in the same way after being subjected to preemptive arrests and controls. KP’s electorate were tired as well, but the effort it made was rewarded with abandonment and careless endangerment when the party leadership abruptly left both protests in late 2024. A year later, CM Gandapur was asked to resign . There was also resentment over the comparatively limited mobilisation from Punjab. Workers from KP were being asked to shoulder risks that supporters elsewhere were either unwilling or unable to assume. The official explanation for Gandapur’s resignation centred on the deteriorating security situation and disagreements over counterterrorism policy, but the failures of 2024 had already weakened his political standing. The larger problem survived his departure. PTI’s electoral mandate in KP remained substantial, but its capacity to convert that mandate into sustained national mobilisation was less certain. Electoral popularity and street power are different political assets. A party can retain the overwhelming loyalty of its voters while finding that those same voters are unwilling to risk arrest, injury or death in repeated attempts at confrontation. That distinction is central to the present crisis. It is entirely possible that a large proportion of KP’s electorate would vote for PTI again in 2029. That does not establish that the same electorate will respond to every call for another march on Islamabad. The failures of 2024, the disappointment with the leadership and the personal costs of confrontation have changed the calculation for at least some of its supporters. Yet PTI has frequently negotiated as though the political circumstances of 2014 still prevail, and every neighbourhood can be mobilised on command. The risk is that the party mistakes enduring loyalty to Imran Khan for an unlimited willingness to undertake increasingly costly political action. Its strategy has become difficult to revise, partly because the organisation itself has become increasingly fragmented. The division The state has not succeeded in producing a decisive split in PTI through defections. The party has nevertheless experienced substantial organic internal division. Imran Khan’s family, ideological loyalists, pragmatists, provincial politicians and competing organisational factions have struggled to establish authority in his absence. They have not had the discipline for their disagreements not to become public, weakening the possibility of a coherent alternative strategy. The only strategy capable of commanding broad agreement has often been the one Imran Khan pursued when he was free. But that strategy was developed in a different political environment, when PTI enjoyed greater institutional access and faced a state whose response to political mobilisation was less restrictive. The party has also overestimated the practical importance of international support. Expectations that foreign governments, including a returning Donald Trump administration, might intervene decisively on Khan’s behalf were never a substitute for domestic political negotiation. The diaspora has presented another complication. Overseas PTI supporters have sustained the party’s international visibility and political messaging, but sections of its external support base have also resisted compromises that might appear insufficiently loyal to Khan. Those living outside Pakistan do not necessarily bear the same immediate costs as party workers, officeholders and families confronting the state at home. This is not an argument against the diaspora’s political participation. It is an argument about the consequences of allowing those least exposed to the costs of confrontation to exercise disproportionate influence over the terms of compromise. In KP, these pressures contributed to an increasingly confrontational political vocabulary. References to Bangladesh’s history , suggestions that the provincial budget might be withheld to produce a constitutional crisis, and proposals involving direct engagement with Afghanistan all raised the stakes. Some of these ideas were unlikely to be carried through, they were the bluster of maximalist rhetoric aimed at eliciting pressure. That did not make them harmless though, especially the threat of a province conducting its own foreign policy as soverign. They made it easier for the federal government to see provincial dissent as a challenge to the constitutional order, even when the underlying disagreement was milder than the rhetoric. The clearest example is the controversy over counterterrorism operations in the former tribal areas. Opposition to another major military operation should not automatically be interpreted as sympathy for militants. Communities in the merged districts have lived through displacement, the destruction of homes and livelihoods, and the prolonged uncertainty of returning to places that had ceased to resemble the homes they left. Their demand to be consulted before another operation is grounded in that experience. For families who have already lost homes, businesses and years of ordinary life, assurances that displacement will be temporary are no longer sufficient. Many residents also question the durability of earlier security gains, particularly when militant activity subsequently returned to areas that had been cleared at enormous human cost by inviting them back. PTI has not always articulated these concerns effectively when they conflated these with demands of the release of Imran Khan. This unfortunately obscured the legitimate demands of the population it represents. But the underlying argument deserves to be taken seriously: a security operation that depends on the cooperation of local communities cannot treat their fears as evidence of disloyalty. A dangerous neighbourhood Pakistan is operating in a more dangerous neighbourhood than it was when PTI first assumed power in KP in 2013. The military confrontation with India in May 2025 demonstrated how quickly a terrorist attack and subsequent military retaliation could escalate into direct conflict between two nuclear-armed states. The crisis involved strikes against military targets and created risks that extended well beyond the immediate battlefield. To the west, relations with Afghanistan have deteriorated from uneasy coexistence into recurring military confrontation. Pakistan has carried out cross-border strikes against what it identifies as militant sanctuaries. These disputes have produced armed exchanges, disrupted border communities and further complicated the security situation in KP. The wider Middle East adds another layer of uncertainty. Israel’s expanding regional confrontations and its security relationships with India are relevant to Pakistan’s strategic calculations, particularly when viewed against Pakistan’s established diplomatic position on Palestine. In such circumstances, effective coordination between federal and provincial authorities becomes more important, while political confrontation makes that coordination harder. But is this a legitimate canvass for an emergency? The federal government cannot expect unquestioning provincial compliance merely by invoking national security. The provincial government cannot treat every security initiative as an extension of its political dispute with Islamabad. Both have obligations that extend beyond their immediate political interests. PTI’s failure to build broader coalitions has made this confrontation more difficult to manage. The party has historically preferred strategies that demonstrate the moral certainty of its position, including electoral boycotts and resignations, even when those decisions have weakened its institutional influence. In the present circumstances, coalition-building was arguably more valuable than another attempt to occupy D-Chowk. A PTI whose street mobilisation had weakened needed the support of parties such as JUI-F and other political actors capable of broadening the dispute beyond the fate of Imran Khan. This loss of the street made keeping the provincial government exceptionally important. Even as its national mobilisation capacity weakened, PTI retained the administrative and political resources of KP. The chief minister’s office gave it visibility, authority and the ability to sustain political activity that an opposition party operating without provincial power would find much harder to organise. The distinction between legitimate government activity and partisan mobilisation therefore became increasingly contested. Orders by the Peshawar and Islamabad High Courts restricting the use of public resources for political protests reduced the room for treating provincial administrative machinery as an extension of party organisation. The pressure was no longer confined to political leaders. Civil servants and police officers faced increasingly explicit expectations that they should not facilitate partisan protests through official resources. This mattered because the institutional advantages of holding provincial office were becoming more difficult to deploy. A mobilisation that could be restricted within KP itself would face considerable difficulties reaching Islamabad. The trigger So why has the Federal Government finally pulled the trigger? Security deterioration supplied the stated constitutional justification. The confrontation over provincial authority, political mobilisation and the limits of federal tolerance supplied its immediate political context. The decision has now changed the incentives for everyone involved. PTI has lost its provincial government, but the federal authorities have also relieved it of the immediate responsibility of governing KP. This is the central paradox of the intervention. For years, PTI had to reconcile its position as a party of confrontation with its obligations as the government of a province facing terrorism, fiscal constraints and difficult relations with the federation. Its opponents could point to failures in policing, administration and economic management. PTI could blame Islamabad, but it could not entirely escape responsibility for the province it governed – such are the dangers of incumbency. Now Governor’s rule changes that calculation. The federal government and the establishment now assume a much greater share of responsibility for what happens in KP. They have reduced PTI’s ability to use the provincial government as an instrument of political mobilisation, but they have also reduced the extent to which PTI can be held directly accountable for provincial administration during the intervention. Every administrative failure, disruption in services or deterioration in security risks becoming an argument against the intervention. Every improvement, meanwhile, will be claimed by the federal authorities as evidence that their decision was necessary. PTI does not need to demonstrate that it could govern better under the new arrangement. It needs to persuade its supporters that the elected government was displaced and that the federal authorities have failed to justify the consequences. The asymmetry is important. The federal government faces a considerably more demanding test. It must demonstrate that extraordinary constitutional intervention can deliver results that ordinary provincial government could not. That means improvements in security, administrative performance and the everyday conditions of people living in KP. It must also demonstrate that the intervention is constitutionally defensible and proportionate to the circumstances that prompted it. Success in administration would strengthen the political argument for the decision. It would not, by itself, settle the constitutional question. An intervention cannot acquire legality retrospectively merely because some of its outcomes are favourable. Nor can political success be measured solely by the restoration of order in Islamabad. Preventing another march on D-Chowk may address an immediate federal concern, but it does little to resolve the insecurity of communities in southern KP or the governance challenges confronting the province. Recent political history offers a warning about the burden of raised expectations. After Imran Khan’s removal in 2022, supporters of the succeeding political arrangement expected a more competent management of the economy. The caretaker period that followed did not produce the transformation many had anticipated. Economic conditions remained difficult, and the political cost of unmet expectations was substantial. The same danger now confronts those assuming responsibility for KP. PTI’s record in the province stretches back to 2013. It has had ample opportunity to establish its own standards of governance, and its performance deserves scrutiny. But replacing an elected government through extraordinary constitutional measures raises expectations that the replacement arrangement will achieve something demonstrably better. That is an exceptionally demanding proposition in a province facing persistent militancy, displacement, unemployment, fiscal dependence and difficult terrain. It is also a proposition that cannot be fulfilled by security measures alone. A durable improvement would require political legitimacy, functioning civilian institutions and a relationship with local communities that extends beyond the demands of counterterrorism. The possibility of renewed protest remains. Removing PTI from provincial office may strengthen its account of political exclusion and give its supporters a grievance around which to organise. Whether that produces sustained mobilisation is uncertain. The disappointments of 2024 have not disappeared, and the willingness to vote for PTI should not be mistaken for a willingness to participate in another confrontation. But the removal of governmental responsibility changes the party’s incentives. PTI may find it easier to reject compromises when it no longer bears the immediate costs of administering the province. The federal government may therefore discover that it has constrained one source of PTI’s power while strengthening another source of its political appeal. Constitutionally, governor’s rule under Article 234 is limited to six months, with parliamentary approval required for its continuation within that period. The simultaneous invocation of Article 232 creates a more complicated legal situation, but it does not automatically eliminate the limitations attached to Article 234. Any attempt to prolong extraordinary federal control would have to confront those distinctions. PTI consequently retains several possible courses of action. It can challenge the intervention in court, attempt to mobilise opposition through protests, or negotiate a new political arrangement that preserves its long-term position while accepting the limits of its immediate power. None of these is without difficulty. Legal proceedings may be prolonged or unsuccessful. Street protests may fail to achieve their objectives while imposing further costs on supporters. Negotiation would require a willingness to accept outcomes short of PTI’s maximal demands, and a party whose internal factions disagree over the meaning of compromise may struggle to sustain such an approach. The federal authorities face choices of their own. If the intervention fails to achieve its stated objectives, they may seek to extend extraordinary measures or consider further restrictions on PTI, including renewed efforts to prohibit the party’s activities. Such measures would introduce additional legal, political and polarisation risks. There is also an external dimension in these tough times. In a country already exposed to confrontation with India and instability along the Afghan border, prolonged internal political exclusion can create opportunities for hostile actors to exploit public grievances. To be clear, that is a risk to be assessed, not a licence to attribute domestic dissent to foreign sponsorship. The deeper question is whether Pakistan’s political institutions can still produce a negotiated settlement between parties that increasingly regard compromise as surrender. For PTI, the challenge is to recognise that electoral popularity does not confer unlimited bargaining power because that is poor strategy which is not serving them well anymore given how much is stacked against it, and that preserving a political movement may require a different strategy from the one that sustained it during Imran Khan’s years in opposition. For the federal government and establishment, the challenge is to recognise that administrative control does not necessarily suppress a mobilisation does not settle the grievances from which it emerged. Both sides have repeatedly demonstrated an ability to impose costs on the other. Neither has yet demonstrated a convincing ability to end the confrontation. But Governor’s rule changes the distribution of those costs. It also changes the burden of accountability. PTI has lost the government it regarded as its last institutional stronghold. The federal authorities have acquired direct responsibility for a province whose difficulties are unlikely to yield to extraordinary powers alone. The next six months will test the proposition that federal control can succeed where elected provincial government was judged to have failed. The result will depend on measurable outcomes, the legality of the intervention and the ability to restore a functioning political relationship. Unfortunately, in Pakistan, a mandate, power or success have never been entirely synonymous. What’s changed now is that the federal government is willing to impose enhanced costs on the PTI – and it’s unlikely to stop here because PTI’s electoral strength, organisational capacity and ability to mobilise protesters are no longer necessarily moving in tandem. The federal government has taken away the PTI’s power, but also taken away their reasons for restraint while burdening the new government with extraordinary expectations of delivery to justify the use of emergency provisions.

articles.title: Pakistan Army deployed in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa in aid of civil power
articles.description: ISLAMABAD: The federal government on Sunday authorised the deployment of Pakistan Army troops and assets in aid of civil power in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, after imposing an emergency and governor’s rule in the province. The authorisation of the army deployment was made through Statutory Regulatory Order, issued by the interior ministry on Sunday. According to the order, a copy of which is available with Dawn , the federal government authorised the deployment of army troops and assets in aid of civil power for the “safety of life, security of persons and property of citizens as well as security of government installations” in the province. The authorisation lasts for the duration of the proclamation issued regarding the imposition of an emergency and governor’s rule. The notification cited powers conferred to the government under Article 245 of the Constitution. KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi, in consultation with the Military Operations Directorate at General Headquarters in Rawalpindi, would determine the number of troops and assets necessary, the notification added. Copies of the order were forwarded to the president’s secretary, prime minister’s adviser, the KP governor’s secretary, the Military Operations Directorate GHQ Rawalpindi, the KP home secretary, the inspector general of police (IGP) in the province, the Peshawar High Court registrar and other officials. The emergency imposition comes a day after PM Shehbaz met President Zardari and discussed the country’s overall security situation. That meeting came amid heightened tensions between the PML-N-led federal government and the KP government led by the PTI — which is in opposition in the Centre. They have been at odds over various issues, particularly on the counterterrorism policy, which was one of the main reasons behind the breakdown of their Oct 3 talks . Police guard a road leading to Red Zone, in Peshawar on October 11, 2026. — Reuters The PTI has said it was being left out of security decisions concerning KP, which the Centre has denied . It also calls for reviewing the counterterrorism policy and opposes military operations. On the other hand, the Centre has been criticising the KP government’s efforts to combat terrorism in the province and objects to its stance on dialogue with the Afghan Taliban. Shipping containers block roads Shipping containers were placed around the city of Peshawar to block roads after the imposition of the emergency. Containers were placed near Peshawar’s railway station to block the routes towards Khyber Bazaar, Shoba Bazaar and beyond. They were also placed near Edwardes College to block entry to Jail Road and Malik Saad Shaheed Flyover, while people were turned away from Sher Shah Suri Road as it was reported to be completely closed. Police were reportedly deployed in significant numbers, particularly around Governor House. The deployment included personnel called from other districts. Police and personnel of law enforcement agencies (LEAs), including many in plainclothes, were seen patrolling the roads leading to Governor House, the central police office, Peshawar police headquarters and other government installations largely located in the Red Zone, a correspondent reported. Vehicles with tinted glasses, police mobile vans, armored personnel carriers and other LEA vehicles were reportedly the only transport visible in and around the cantonment area, with life at a standstill and the area appearing deserted. Another correspondent reported that the road leading to Khyber Road was shuttered by a container and the traffic control gate closed. A large number of police personnel were also seen around Surey Pul, a favoured spot for protesters. Grand Trunk (GT) Road was blocked by containers at Firdous Chowk and the correspondent reported a large number of police personnel in the area. Only pedestrians were allowed to move ahead. Additionally, containers near Bala Hisar Fort and outside the Pakistan International Airlines (PIA) office on Arbab Road blocked entry towards Mall Road. A vehicle moves past a shipping container used to block a road leading to the Red Zone, in Peshawar on October 11, 2026. — Reuters Only official vehicles were being allowed to travel from Governor House towards the Chief Minister’s House, while tight security was reported on Sahibzada Abdul Qayyum road where they are located. The Civil Secretariat was seen to be deserted. Royal Artillery (RA) Bazaar has been closed, while Saddar remains partially open. Additionally, Peshawar’s Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) stations were reported to be shuttered by Dawn ’s correspondent. The stretch of Khyber Road connecting to University Road and Airport Road at Aman Chowk was reported to be open but with low traffic. A large police contingent was seen at Aman Chowk. Meanwhile, University Road was blocked by containers at Tehkal, and containers at Stadium Chowk allowed for only single-file passage of vehicles on both sides. Earlier, traffic jams were reported due to the closure of Khyber Road, which connects GT Road with the eastern side of University Road and serves as the main artery and choke point. The resulting diversions created pressure on auxiliary roads. The area is part of the cantonment, and the Red Zone contains important installations such as the Corps Commander’s House, civil secretariat, central police office, CM Secretariat, CM House and Governor House. All telecoms services, including landline and DSL, are reported to be suspended in the provincial capital. The city had witnessed a nearly 48-hour mobile service blackout just days ago, on account of the presence of the PTI in the city for its long march . With networks suspended, people faced immense issues in withdrawing money from bank accounts, as ATMs remained out of service for the entire day. Aside from the suspension of cellular network and broadband services, however, the situation remained normal for those living on Kohat Road, Charsadda Road, GT Road beyond Pir Zakorhi Bridge, and the area bordering the Khyber district, as well as others on the outskirts of the provincial capital. Vehicles of the armed forces were also reported to be patrolling cantonment areas and a heavy deployment of police was reported in both the city and its outskirts including Kohat Road, GT Road, University Road and Warsak Road. Separately, a holiday has been declared for schools, colleges and universities in the district on Monday (Oct 12), according to a notification issued by the deputy commissioner of Peshawar. “It is hereby notified that all educational institutions, both public and private, including schools, colleges and universities, shall remain closed on October 12, 2026 (Monday) located within the territorial jurisdiction of District Peshawar,” the notification said. On Saturday, KP Inspector General of Police (IGP) Zulfiqar Hameed put district police on alert for possible violent protests and sabotage in the event of an emergency in the province, emphasising caution in the use of force. Police personnel stand guard near shipping containers blocking a road leading to the Red Zone in Peshawar on October 11, 2026. — Reuters A notification issued by the IGP’s office directed not only officers in Peshawar but also district police officers (DPOs), sub-divisional police officers (SDPOs) and even station house officers (SHOs) to personally monitor the situation. It said DPOs could issue appropriate directions, instructions or guidelines to regulate protests and ensure public safety. In the event of violence, they could also take necessary legal action. It added that the use of force was to be carried out on a gradated basis, noting that in the first phase, protesters should be clearly warned against violence before police began to use forceful measures.
