articles.title: Peshawar becomes city of containers
articles.description: PESHAWAR: Despite being in throes of violence for the past many decades, Peshawar, the capital of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, has most of the time enjoyed political stability. The violence came and went but political stability was always there despite the sabre-rattling with federal government and marches on Islamabad. A semblance of understanding between Islamabad and Peshawar, no matter how little, was still there. However, all this changed on Sunday after the imposition of governor’s rule and emergency in the province. The night before, skies of Peshawar poured buckets, flooding roads and drenching the city; however, the Sunday morning was warm and sunny. Yet it started with a sense of dread as uncertainty hung heavy over the city. The telltale signs of not everything is good dawned upon after reaching for telephone, the ritual everyone does upon waking up. The impending doom was there for all to see: no mobile signals. Routine journey in the city turns into hectic exercise as governor’s rule imposed The city had witnessed a nearly 48 hours long mobile service blackout just days ago owing to PTI protest march. Outside, the stations of Peshawar Bus Transit (BRT), whose buses come on road early in the morning, remained shut. The GT Road was closed at Firdous Chowk by placing shipping containers. A large number of police personnel was deputed at this spot. Only pedestrians were allowed to move ahead on GT Road and a large number of cops were sitting outside the shuttered shops on GT Road between Hospital Road and Firdous Chowk, also called the Malik Saad Shaheed Chowk. A bearded cop on the road stopped me and handed over a shopping bag containing fried peas. Perplexed, I looked at him and he turned his back toward me, asking me to put the peas into the back pocket of his bulletproof vest. The gates of Bala Hisar Fort, which houses the headquarters of Frontier Corps North, were shuttered and a contingent of policemen was resting on the footpath. A few steps from here just outside the KP Assembly is Surey Chowk, from where GT Road leads commuters to Khyber Road, which houses the city red zone. Police guard a road leading to the Red Zone, in Peshawar. — Reuters The road leading to Khyber Road was blocked with containers and the gate erected to control traffic was also closed. A large number of cops were milling around Surey Pul Square, which is the most favoured spot for protesters of all kinds and hues. At the end of Justice Rustam Kiyani Road near central jail , where the artery leads to Sher Shah Suri Road, an old armoured personnel carrier was parked and two cops there were telling walkers not to proceed further. A few of us ignored their warnings but just next to MPA Hostel, a large contingent of cops yelled at us to go back and take detour through Shoba Bazaar. The Jail Pul, which connects Sher Shah Suri Road with Khyber Bazaar, was also closed. I met an acquaintance there who offered to take me through Civil Secretariat and we entered the Police Road and secretariat without any hassle. Civil Secretariat, the beating heart of KP government, was completely deserted with a few cars parked outside the chief secretary office. On Sahibzada Abdul Qayyum Road, where houses of minister and governor are located, security was very tight and police personnel were checking everyone heading towards both the houses. From the distance, I saw a large number of vehicles parked outside the Governor’s Houses. Walking the road in the opposite direction towards Khyber Road, I saw an APC, a prison van and truck carrying riot police, heading in the direction of Chief Minister House. After a few minutes’ walk, a barricade was erected on Khyber Road near Army Stadium and when I approached the personnel standing there and explained that I needed to cross to the other side, a plainclothes youth holding a radio just sputtered a series of “no, no, no, no. You must go back. This road is closed and we cannot open this barrier.” I stood there in plain confusion thinking of what to do. No question of going back and with no telephone, I was unable to approach any official. Then as a last resort, I pleaded with paramilitary personnel to let me out and one of them signalled another guard to open the gate for me. But the plainclothes again jumped in front of me and said no. Then the other, standing behind laughed, perhaps, they were enjoying my confusion or saw fear on my face. “How rudimentary freedom is,” muses one of the characters in JM Coetzee. Waiting for the Barbarians. Little did we realise how important is the ability to move freely without any fear, without being stopped. Outside the stretch of Khyber Road, connecting University Road and Airport Road, Amn Chowk was open but there was little traffic. A large contingent of cops was present at Amn Chowk, previously called the Gora Qabristan Chowk. The University Road was blocked at Tehkal with containers, a biker told me. There were also containers on Stadium Chowk only letting cars in a single line on both sides. Saddar Bazaar was partially open oblivious to changing political fortunes and game of thrones which was currently under way just a stone’s throw away. A container was also placed on Arbab Road, connecting Mall Road to Saddar Road, with a few cops lazing under a tree outside the Presentation Convent School. For many years, marchers from Peshawar used to result into turning the federal capital into a fortress of containers but this time Islamabad instead sent containers to Peshawar. It is to be seen how long these containers are going to stay here. In the afternoon, the internet also died. Published in Dawn, October 12th, 2026

articles.title: States of exception: what the Constitution, 3 court rulings and 50 years say about the KP emergency
articles.description: ‘Sovereign is he who decides on the exception,’ wrote the notorious German thinker Carl Schmitt in 1922. Or, put simply, whoever gets to decide when the rules stop applying is the one actually in charge. Gifted with a big brain and sharp turn of phrase, Schmitt went on to become a noted critic of parliament, constitutionalism, and liberal democracy. For a time, the age was also his: in the ’20s back then, much like the ’20s now, such subjects had fallen out of fashion. But as a much-quoted critique of Mr Schmitt went, ‘His preferred cure turned out to be infinitely worse than the disease.’ Why did this happen? So too, the centre tells us, that the ministry of Sohail Afridi in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa is the disease, and emergency the cure . As to what kind of disease, we can’t be sure. The centre claims militancy; terror bleeding back into the headlines. But if that is the main case to be made, everything that attaches to Sohail Afridi in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa also attaches to Sarfraz Bugti in Balochistan, a province nearly half the country’s landmass. The unity regime is unhappy with such comparisons; apples and bowling balls, they say: Bugti’s ministers are cooperating with the centre, whereas Afridi’s are Taliban sympathisers. That, too, is an odd distinction: as Maulana Fazl-ur-Rehman pointed out, Nawaz League had opposed Musharraf’s terror wars not too long ago, and no one had sent home the maulana’s coalition for putting up similar opposition in the same province after 2002. Then there’s the timing: militancy has been resurgent in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa for years. Yet the din of emergency only sounded when Afridi announced he would hit the streets over access to his jailed leader, Imran Khan. Bloody terror attacks , and there were several, were never the trigger point. If there was an explanation, it came — intentionally or otherwise — from prime minister Shehbaz Sharif the day emergency was declared. Sharif cited the PTI’s Long March protests at length: ‘Islamabad ki charhai…ka napak mansooba ,’ was how he described it to his cabinet, before thanking Maulana Fazl for trying to keep the peace between the centre and the PTI (the maulana has since blamed the centre for backpedalling on its commitment). ‘It’s now or never,’ concluded Sharif, ‘…History will remember us for such decisions, in this way or that way.’ But history is already heading in that way, not this one: displacing a duly elected provincial government with a two-thirds majority is certainly memorable, but not for reasons the prime minister may suspect. After all, it’s a question of perspective: when Asif Zardari imposed governor’s rule in Punjab in February 2009, then-deposed chief minister Shehbaz Sharif had taken a much poorer view of the issue. The same president is now doing it on the same man’s advice in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa: the unity regime has imposed both emergency as well as governor’s rule. Breaking down emergency These two provisions of the Constitution — emergency under Article 232, and governor’s rule under Article 234 — have different purposes and different tests. Exceptions exist in the affairs of states, and they are a part of the law for a reason: Pervez Musharraf was sentenced to death not for the act of declaring emergency in 2007, but for expressly refusing to use the Constitution to do it. That said, there are rules to follow: emergency requires the threat of war or external aggression, or an internal disturbance beyond Peshawar’s power to control. Governor’s rule, by contrast, is the answer to a narrower problem: when a provincial government can no longer function under the Constitution. Both have trade-offs: while the provincial assembly retains some of its lawmaking powers under emergency, those powers can be handed off to Islamabad under governor’s rule. Yet whereas governor’s rule cannot be extended beyond six months, emergency — subject to parliamentary approval — does not contain any hard outer limit within the text. Crucially, emergency also lends the centre an umbrella to suspend fundamental rights under a third provision, Article 233. For reasons obvious, the unity regime has decided to go for broke, and push both buttons 232 and 234. By mixing two very distinct provisions in the same soup, it can try and claim the best of both worlds: emergency that can go on and on, that can swallow up fundamental rights, and that can, for the present, shutter the assembly via the governor. Of course, opposition protests, at least at the time of the proclamation, neither amount to external aggression nor to internal disturbance required for emergency. They also do not speak to the breakdown of provincial government required for governor’s rule. This is quite apart from the fact that going for a combo deal is a strange step: Article 232 assumes a provincial government overwhelmed by events, and leaves its assembly standing. Article 234 says the government itself cannot function constitutionally. It is hard to imagine both being true (and, in any event, neither is). Plus, the unity regime is diving over guardrails it once built itself: the Eighteenth Amendment requires a resolution of the province’s own assembly for an internal emergency. Failing that, each house of parliament must approve within 10 days. Zardari, who signed off on the original amendment once upon a time, has used the backdoor: at no point did the province consent. What becomes of the PTI government? Afridi’s ministry may have been displaced for now, but it cannot be ousted outright. That can only happen when he loses the legislature’s confidence: as a Supreme Court concurrence put it in Pir Sabir Shah v. Federation in 1994, ‘The president, therefore, cannot dismiss the chief minister and the provincial cabinet in exercise of his power under Article 234.’ Afridi thus returns the second the proclamation of governor’s rule is lifted, per Sabir Shah , along with his cabinet and assembly. As for ‘history remembering’, Sharif has his own party men to thank for securing such a verdict in 1994, that too against the Bhutto-Zardaris’ attempt at ouster. ‘History will remember’: what have the courts held? A year after Sabir Shah , when the same PPP thought to remove chief minister Manzoor Wattoo in Punjab, it again ended in tears: Shehbaz Sharif, then leader of the opposition, even raised the alleged plot in the provincial assembly. The Lahore High Court ruled against the PPP’s power grab: to impose governor’s rule under Article 234, a ‘breakdown of constitutional machinery’ was a must. No such breakdown was in the offing then in Punjab, nor now in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. As for emergency, the test is even starker. Again, the ruling regime would know: in May 1998, the prime minister’s brother Nawaz Sharif had imposed emergency under Article 232 and suspended fundamental rights under Article 233, right after Pakistan and India’s nuclear tests. But Nawaz’s emergency was challenged in the Supreme Court by former president Farooq Leghari and one Imran Khan, described (in a strange echo of network television’s ongoing ban) as ‘chairman of a political party Tehrik-e-Insaf’. While the Court ruled in favour of emergency, it did so explicitly on the basis of ‘imminent danger of external aggression’. In 1998, that meant mushroom clouds. In 2026, it means Sohail Afridi’s caravan meandering down from Peshawar. Not least, it felt the government’s claims of lawlessness in Sindh and sectarian killings in Punjab didn’t count as actionable internal disturbances, and that Islamabad had no good reason to suspend fundamental rights. The Court struck down the suspension. Compared to the present, context is also important. Under Article 232, Chief Justice Ajmal Mian held in Leghari , ‘the existence of the nation itself is at stake’. In 1998, that meant mushroom clouds. In 2026, it means Sohail Afridi’s caravan meandering down from Peshawar. Let the voter decide The unity regime’s latest disaster is not only self-inflicted, it is also self-defeating. Back when Zulfikar Ali Bhutto dismissed the National Awami Party’s ministry in Balochistan in 1973, it was for reasons that rhymed with today’s: terror, disloyalty, and the backing of hostile powers. Yet the only thing Bhutto managed to destroy was his opposition. After Quetta fell, the NAP’s coalition in the frontier (led, in yet another irony, by Maulana Fazl’s father Mufti Mahmood) resigned in protest. A four-year insurgency followed in one province, and mayhem and murder in the other. It turns out that displacing an elected government in a restive land has been tried before. The only way through, in both Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan, is through greater representation, not less. When Pakistan did prevail against insurgency in the previous round, it was because of a hard-won consensus between state and society. That consensus is fracturing. Emergency will be its accelerant.

articles.title: DPM Dar defends emergency and governor's rule in KP, says measures not politically motivated
articles.description: A day after the government imposed governor’s rule and emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar defended the move, saying it was not politically motivated but instead taken to curb terrorism. DPM Dar made the comments while addressing a seminar in Islamabad, a day after the federal government imposed emergency under Article 232 and the governor’s rule under Article 234 in KP. The Cabinet recommended the move, citing the PTI-led provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism”. Referring to “recent developments” in the country, Dar said, “It is not a political move; it is surely against the menace of terrorism which that province (KP) has been hit with in the past decade and a half.” He asked if the Centre could “keep sleeping and looking towards one another because it may be deemed as a political move? “No, it is not. I can guarantee you.” Dar recalled that he negotiated with PTI in 2014 during a sit-in in Islamabad. Defending the move further, Dar held it was the federal government’s responsibility to take such steps “once it is totally determined that there is no solution other than what we have done yesterday”. He stressed that the ruling party PML-N bore a “heavy political cost” when the country was on the brink of default in 2022. Dar recalled that the government had to take difficult structural measures. “Political cost was paid, unpopularity was there, and we recovered a lot because we saved the country from the brink of default.” Dar said the government “had no choice but to take the measures we took yesterday, and we will implement it in totality”. He hoped the progress would show in the time ahead. “I am sure the province will be quite happy to see peace restored, their lives are safe and the radicalisation [will end]. Information Minister Attaullah Tarar also spoke at the seminar and defended the federal government’s actions. Following the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in KP, the federal government also authorised the deployment of Pakistan Army troops and assets in aid of civil power in the province. On the ground, shipping containers were placed around the city of Peshawar to block several roads, with heavy police deployment. On Sunday, federal ministers alleged that the PTI-led government in KP had a “nexus” with terrorist groups, as the Centre explained that the province’s security situation necessitated the imposition of emergency there. The Centre and the PTI have been at odds over various issues, particularly on the counterterrorism policy, which was one of the main reasons behind the breakdown of their October 3 talks . The previous night, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi had posted on X along the same lines, saying that the decision was “neither a political decision nor an easy step”. He added, “It was a difficult CONSTITUTIONAL course made necessary by the circumstances on the ground. “When every avenue for cooperation has been exhausted, the Constitution and Pakistan should be the priority.” He reiterated that the government and its allies had “exhausted every avenue of parliamentary engagement, direct dialogue and back channel diplomacy”. “KP has borne a heavy burden of terrorism and our security forces and civilians have made immense sacrifices. In these circumstances, cooperation should have been the priority,” Naqvi said. Pakistan’s desire for peace must not be misconstrued as weakness: Tarar Tarar, in his address, spoke of counterterrorism, particularly the threat emanating from Afghan soil. He said that Pakistan wanted peaceful coexistence with Afghanistan, but went on to warn that the country’s desire for peace must not be “misconstrued as weakness”. Tarar said Pakistan had been at the forefront of the war against terrorism, paying a heavy price in terms of human lives and economic losses. “No other nation in the world can say that it has lost more than 90,000 lives in the war against terrorism,” he said, adding that Pakistan had suffered economic losses exceeding $100 billion. “When we represent Pakistan at conferences like this one, we stand before you as ambassadors of peace,” he said, describing Pakistan as a symbol of defiance against violent extremism and resilience against terrorism. He said Pakistan had acted as a shield between terrorists and the rest of the world, adding that the sacrifices made by Pakistanis in the fight against terrorism contributed to global peace. “When a Pakistani lays down his or her life fighting terrorism, it is not only to make Pakistan a safer place, but also to contribute to global peace,” he said. Tarar said Pakistan’s recent role in mediating between the United States and Iran had demonstrated its commitment to peace. He said Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, DPM Dar and Chief of Army Staff and Chief of Defence Forces Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir had made immense efforts to facilitate the mediation process, which had received international recognition. Given its strategic location and shared border with Afghanistan, Pakistan had always sought regional stability, he said, adding that a peaceful and stable Afghanistan would promote trade with Central Asia, attract foreign investment and strengthen regional cooperation and connectivity. He said Pakistan had participated in negotiations and engaged with the Afghan interim government to convey its desire for peace and prosperity in the region, particularly in Afghanistan. The rallies in the capital come after weeks of opposition mobilisation following allegations of misconduct during a nationwide voter roll revision that critics say could benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling party. The Election Commission of India, which oversees the voting process in the world’s most populous nation, has denied wrongdoing. Abhijeet Dipke, founder of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), and two other leaders were released Sunday, one day after they were detained when they landed in New Delhi to take part in a protest at the Jantar Mantar site in the heart of the city. Thousands of protesters have been detained since Saturday, according to the group and media reports. “We will not back down,” Saurav Das, another top CJP leader, told reporters after his release. “We urge people to come out and carry out peaceful protests,” he added, vowing to continue until Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar resigns. Smaller rallies took place in Delhi on Sunday. Dozens of protesters were detained near Jantar Mantar, which remained blocked off, AFP journalists witnessed. Police have not commented on the detentions. Reporters Without Borders (RSF) said at least 16 journalists had also been detained, calling the police actions “unacceptable”. “Covering events of public interest is not a crime,” RSF said in a statement. “It is their job.” In July, protests organised by the CJP over exam irregularities forced the resignation of the education minister, marking a rare climbdown by Modi’s administration. ‘Important show up’ Ahead of Saturday’s rally, authorities mounted a sweeping security operation across the capital, shutting down metro stations and more than 200 trains while imposing a ban on public gatherings in several areas. The Supreme Court, hearing petitions challenging Saturday’s detentions and other security measures, directed the authorities to ensure protesters gathering peacefully were not detained illegally. “Detention shall only be after following a legal procedure,” Justice Joymalya Bagchi said in oral remarks. The court also ordered authorities to ensure there was no disruption to internet connectivity as seen on Saturday. ‘An embarrassment to India’ The CJP has emerged as one of the most significant political challenges to Modi during his third term in power, winning millions of followers on social media since it was launched in May as a satirical party. Soon after his release, the CJP’s Dipke took aim at Modi, calling him “an embarrassment to India”. “Never has this country seen a bigger coward and bully,” he said in a social media post. The revision of voter rolls resulted in more than 133 million names being removed from electoral lists, according to media reports. Critics say the measure has disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims, potentially benefiting Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party. Election authorities say the move was aimed at eliminating duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries. The detention of protesters on Saturday triggered sharp criticism and accusations that Modi’s government was stifling dissent. The UN human rights office called for the immediate and unconditional release of all those “arbitrarily detained” in Delhi — a comment the Indian government called “misplaced”. Rahul Gandhi, leader of the opposition Congress party, said he was planning to march to the Supreme Court on Monday with “every single person who believes in democracy”. “There is nothing to fear,” he said on social media. “These cowards can do absolutely nothing to us. “
